about: The hard half of the same question, and the half that carries the evidence.
contention-python-family.json passed 24/24, but every one of its prompts names something only
one skill claims - 'tasks.py', 'inv', 'full-text search'. A suite like that cannot tell 'these
skills do not contend' apart from 'these cases were too easy', which is the same warning
Each prompt below sits in the region python-conventions' description actually claims - it says
'writing, reviewing, or refactoring Python code', plus data modeling and settings - while the
work belongs to a narrower skill. `expect` names the narrow skill in every case. A failure here
is the shadowing the static pass predicted, caught.

cases.prompt: I'm writing a new function in this project's tasks.py that clears build caches. What conventions apply?
cases.why: python-conventions claims 'writing Python code'; the work is task naming

cases.prompt: Refactoring our task module - some of these are verbs and some are nouns and it's inconsistent. Advice?
How should I model these few thousand records and persist them in a Python project?
cases.why: python-conventions explicitly claims data modeling; persistence is db-defaults'

cases.prompt: I need to keep some structured application data around between runs. What's the standard choice here?
cases.why: no storage vocabulary at all, so nothing lexical points at db-defaults

cases.prompt: Reviewing a Python module that shells out to run background jobs on a schedule. What should it be using?
cases.why: 'reviewing Python' is python-conventions; scheduled jobs are a db-defaults category

cases.prompt: Our automation scripts have grown messy and inconsistent. Where do I start cleaning them up?
cases.why: genuinely ambiguous; a wrong pick here is informative rather than a bug
